what: Americold is a real estate investment trust that owns and runs temperature-controlled warehouses, the second largest network of cold storage in the world after Lineage. Its facilities store frozen and chilled food for producers, retailers and distributors in North America, Europe and Asia-Pacific.
customers: Food producers such as Conagra and Kraft Heinz, grocery retailers and distributors that need frozen and refrigerated storage and handling.
money: Fees for storing pallets in its freezers and coolers.
Handling, blast freezing, labelling and other work done on stored goods.
Arranging trucks to move goods between customers and warehouses.
moat: Cold storage is expensive to build and hard to permit, and a warehouse placed near ports, rail lines and food plants is not easily replaced. Customers sign long contracts and rarely move inventory once it is in place.
risks: Occupancy has fallen as food companies cut inventories, and new capacity built in the boom years is competing for customers.
Free cash flow has been negative in 2025 and over the last twelve months because of large development spending.
Debt of $3.3B against $3.0B of equity is high for a REIT whose earnings are under pressure.
Labour is a large share of costs, and wage inflation hits margins.
opportunities: At about $16 and a 5.6% yield, the shares price in a lot of the bad news.
Cold storage capacity is old in many markets, and demand for frozen food keeps growing over time.
Seventeen analysts average a target just above the price, which suggests sentiment is near a low.
New automated warehouses could lower costs once occupancy recovers.
watch: Same-store occupancy and economic occupancy, which show whether demand is returning.
view: Ignore the P/E of 19 on this page. Americold has lost money in most years shown and only shows a trailing profit because of gains and one-off items; for a REIT, the right measure is adjusted funds from operations, and on that basis the shares trade at a low multiple compared with their history. The negative free cash flow comes from building new warehouses, not from the existing ones losing cash.

The problem is demand. Food companies stocked up heavily in 2021 and 2022 and have been running inventories down since, while new capacity built during the boom competes for the same pallets. Occupancy is falling across the industry, and Lineage, the market leader, has had a terrible run since its IPO for the same reason.

This turns on when inventories stop falling. Cold storage is a good long-term business with real barriers, and today’s price reflects a cyclical trough. But the balance sheet is stretched for a company whose earnings are falling, and the dividend depends on occupancy stabilising. I would wait for that sign before buying, and accept that the shares may already have moved by then.
bull: Food inventories rebuild, occupancy recovers and the shares re-rate from trough valuations.
bear: Oversupply lasts longer than expected, the dividend is cut and debt forces asset sales.
